title: Chapter 13 — Literary Characteristics Of Democratic Ages
paragraphs: When a traveler goes into a bookseller's shop in the United States and examines the American books on the shelves, the number of works appears extremely large — while the number of known authors appears, on the contrary, extremely small. He will first meet with a number of elementary treatises meant to teach the rudiments of human knowledge. Most of these books are written in Europe; the Americans reprint them, adapting them to their own country. Next comes an enormous quantity of religious works — Bibles, sermons, edifying anecdotes, controversial theology, and reports of charitable societies. Last appears the long catalogue of political pamphlets. In America, parties do not write books to combat each other's opinions, but pamphlets that are circulated for a day with incredible rapidity and then expire. In the midst of all these obscure productions of the human brain are to be found the more remarkable works of that small number of authors whose names are, or ought to be, known to Europeans.

Although America is perhaps in our day the civilized country where literature is least attended to, a large number of people are nevertheless to be found there who take an interest in the productions of the mind, and who make them, if not the study of their lives, at least the charm of their leisure hours. But England supplies these readers with the larger portion of the books they require. Almost all important English books are republished in the United States. The literary genius of Great Britain still darts its rays into the recesses of the forests of the New World. There is hardly a pioneer's hut that does not contain a few odd volumes of Shakespeare. I remember that I read the feudal play of Henry V for the first time in a log cabin.

Not only do the Americans constantly draw on the treasures of English literature; it may be said with truth that they find the literature of England growing on their own soil. The larger part of that small number of men in the United States engaged in the composition of literary works are English in substance, and still more so in form. Thus they transplant into the midst of democracy the ideas and literary fashions current among the aristocratic nation they have taken as their model. They paint with colors borrowed from foreign manners; and since they hardly ever depict the country they were born in as it really is, they are seldom popular there. The citizens of the United States are themselves so convinced that books are not published for them that, before they can make up their minds about the merit of one of their authors, they generally wait until his fame has been ratified in England — just as with pictures the author of an original is held to be entitled to judge of the merit of a copy. The inhabitants of the United States, then, have at present, strictly speaking, no literature. The only authors I acknowledge as American are the journalists. They are indeed not great writers, but they speak the language of their countrymen and make themselves heard by them. Other authors are aliens; they are to the Americans what the imitators of the Greeks and Romans were to us at the revival of learning — an object of curiosity, not of general sympathy. They amuse the mind, but they do not act upon the manners of the people.

I have already said that this state of things is very far from originating in democracy alone, and that the causes of it must be sought in several peculiar circumstances independent of the democratic principle. If the Americans, retaining the same laws and social condition, had had a different origin and had been transported into another country, I do not doubt that they would have had a literature. Even as they now are, I am convinced that they will eventually have one. But its character will be different from that which marks American literary productions of our time, and that character will be peculiarly its own. Nor is it impossible to trace this character in advance.

I imagine an aristocratic people among whom letters are cultivated. The labors of the mind, as well as the affairs of state, are conducted by a ruling class in society. The literary as well as the political career is almost entirely confined to this class, or to those nearest to it in rank. These premises are enough to give me a key to all the rest. When a small number of the same men are engaged at the same time on the same objects, they easily concert with one another and agree upon certain leading rules meant to govern them all. If the object that attracts the attention of these men is literature, the productions of the mind will soon be subjected by them to precise canons, from which it will no longer be permissible to depart. If these men occupy a hereditary position in the country, they will be naturally inclined not only to adopt a certain number of fixed rules for themselves, but to follow those their forefathers laid down for their own guidance. Their code will be at once strict and traditional. Since they are not necessarily absorbed by the cares of daily life — as they have never been, any more than their fathers were before them — they have learned, over several generations, to take an interest in the labors of the mind. They have learned to understand literature as an art, to love it in the end for its own sake, and to feel a scholar-like satisfaction in seeing men conform to its rules. Nor is this all: the men I am speaking of began, and will end, their lives in easy or affluent circumstances. Hence they have naturally formed a taste for choice gratifications and a love of refined and delicate pleasures. More than that, a kind of indolence of mind and heart, which they often contract in the midst of this long and peaceful enjoyment of so much welfare, leads them to put aside, even from their pleasures, whatever might be too startling or too sharp. They would rather be amused than intensely excited; they want to be interested, but not to be carried away.

Now let us imagine a great number of literary works executed by, or for, the men I have just described, and we shall easily conceive a style of literature in which everything will be regular and prearranged. The slightest work will be carefully finished in its least details; art and labor will be conspicuous everywhere. Each kind of writing will have rules of its own, from which it will not be allowed to swerve, and which distinguish it from all others. Style will be thought of almost as much importance as thought, and form will be no less considered than matter. The diction will be polished, measured, and uniform. The tone of the mind will always be dignified, seldom very animated; and writers will care more to perfect what they produce than to multiply their productions. It will sometimes happen that the members of the literary class, always living among themselves and writing for themselves alone, will lose sight of the rest of the world, which will infect them with a false and labored style. They will lay down minute literary rules for their exclusive use, which will imperceptibly lead them to deviate from common sense and finally to overstep the bounds of nature. By straining after a mode of speech different from the common, they will arrive at a sort of aristocratic jargon hardly less removed from pure language than the coarse dialect of the people. Such are the natural perils of literature under aristocracies. Every aristocracy that keeps itself entirely aloof from the people becomes impotent — a fact as true in literature as in politics. *a

[Footnote a: All this is especially true of aristocratic countries that have long and peacefully been subject to a monarchical government. When liberty prevails in an aristocracy, the higher ranks are constantly obliged to make use of the lower classes; and when they use them, they approach them. This frequently introduces something of a democratic spirit into an aristocratic community. There springs up, moreover, in a privileged body governing with energy and a habitually bold policy, a taste for stir and excitement which must inevitably affect all literary performances.]

Let us now turn the picture around and consider the other side. Let us transport ourselves into the midst of a democracy not unprepared by ancient traditions and present culture to share in the pleasures of the mind. Ranks there are intermingled and confounded; knowledge and power are both infinitely subdivided and, if I may use the expression, scattered on every side. Here, then, is a motley multitude whose intellectual wants must be supplied. These new votaries of the pleasures of the mind have not all received the same education; they do not possess the same degree of culture as their fathers, nor any resemblance to them. In fact, they continually differ from themselves, for they live in a state of incessant change of place, feelings, and fortunes. The mind of each member of the community is therefore unattached to that of his fellow citizens by tradition or by common habits; and they have never had the power, the inclination, or the time to concert together. Yet it is from the bosom of this heterogeneous and agitated mass that authors spring, and from the same source their profits and their fame are distributed. I can without difficulty understand that, in these circumstances, I must expect to meet in the literature of such a people but few of those strict conventional rules accepted by readers and writers in aristocratic ages. If it should happen that the men of some one period agreed upon any such rules, that would prove nothing for the following period — for among democratic nations each new generation is a new people. Among such nations, then, literature will not easily be subjected to strict rules, and it is impossible that any such rules should ever be permanent.

In democracies, it is by no means the case that all the men who cultivate literature have received a literary education. And most of those who have some tinge of belles-lettres are either engaged in politics or in a profession that only allows them to taste the pleasures of the mind occasionally and by stealth. These pleasures, therefore, do not form the principal charm of their lives; they are considered as a transient and necessary recreation amid the serious labors of life. Such a man can never acquire a sufficiently intimate knowledge of the art of literature to appreciate its more delicate beauties, and the minor shades of expression must escape him. Since the time he can devote to letters is very short, he seeks to make the best use of all of it. He prefers books that can be easily procured, quickly read, and that require no learned research to be understood. He asks for beauties that are self-proffered and easily enjoyed. Above all, he must have what is unexpected and new. Accustomed to the struggle, the setbacks, and the monotony of practical life, he requires rapid emotions, startling passages — truths or errors brilliant enough to rouse him up and plunge him at once, as if by violence, into the midst of a subject.

Why should I say more? Who does not understand what is about to follow before I have expressed it? Taken as a whole, literature in democratic ages can never present, as it does in periods of aristocracy, an aspect of order, regularity, science, and art. Its form will, on the contrary, ordinarily be slighted, sometimes despised. Style will frequently be fantastic, incorrect, overburdened, and loose — almost always vehement and bold. Authors will aim at rapidity of execution more than at perfection of detail. Small productions will be more common than bulky books; there will be more wit than erudition, more imagination than depth; and literary performances will bear marks of an untutored and rude vigor of thought, frequently of great variety and singular fertility. The object of authors will be to astonish rather than to please, and to stir the passions more than to charm the taste. Here and there, doubtless, writers will appear who choose a different track, and who, if they are gifted with superior abilities, will succeed in finding readers in spite of their defects or their better qualities. But these exceptions will be rare, and even the authors who so depart from received practice in the main subject of their works will always relapse into it in some lesser details.

I have just depicted two extreme conditions. The transition by which a nation passes from the former to the latter is not sudden but gradual, and marked with shades of very various intensity. In the passage that carries a lettered people from the one to the other, there is almost always a moment when the literary genius of democratic nations has its confluence with that of aristocracies, and both seek to establish their joint sway over the human mind. Such epochs are transient but very brilliant — fertile without exuberance, and animated without confusion. The French literature of the eighteenth century may serve as an example.

I should say more than I mean if I were to assert that the literature of a nation is always subordinate to its social condition and its political constitution. I am aware that, apart from these causes, there are several others that confer certain characteristics on literary productions. But these appear to me to be the chief. The relations that exist between the social and political condition of a people and the genius of its authors are always very numerous: whoever knows the one is never completely ignorant of the other.
